claim: Regions sensitive to specific object categories have been found across the whole ventral temporal cortex (VTC).
source: Regions sensitive to specific object categories as well as organized spatial patterns sensitive to different features have been found across the whole ventral temporal cortex (VTC).
evidence: This is a general statement about existing findings in the field, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Organized spatial patterns sensitive to different features have been found across the whole ventral temporal cortex (VTC).
source: Regions sensitive to specific object categories as well as organized spatial patterns sensitive to different features have been found across the whole ventral temporal cortex (VTC).
evidence: This is a general statement about existing findings in the field, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Within right posterior fusiform face area (pFFA), the posterior portion was biased to eyes.
source: Our results show consistent spatial tuning of face parts across individuals that within right posterior fusiform face area (pFFA) and right occipital face area (OFA), the posterior portion of each region was biased to eyes, while the anterior portion was biased to mouth and chin stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Within right posterior fusiform face area (pFFA), the anterior portion was biased to mouth and chin stimuli.
source: Our results show consistent spatial tuning of face parts across individuals that within right posterior fusiform face area (pFFA) and right occipital face area (OFA), the posterior portion of each region was biased to eyes, while the anterior portion was biased to mouth and chin stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Within right occipital face area (OFA), the posterior portion was biased to eyes.
source: Our results show consistent spatial tuning of face parts across individuals that within right posterior fusiform face area (pFFA) and right occipital face area (OFA), the posterior portion of each region was biased to eyes, while the anterior portion was biased to mouth and chin stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Within right occipital face area (OFA), the anterior portion was biased to mouth and chin stimuli.
source: Our results show consistent spatial tuning of face parts across individuals that within right posterior fusiform face area (pFFA) and right occipital face area (OFA), the posterior portion of each region was biased to eyes, while the anterior portion was biased to mouth and chin stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: The spatial tuning of face parts is consistent across individuals.
source: Our results show consistent spatial tuning of face parts across individuals that within right posterior fusiform face area (pFFA) and right occipital face area (OFA), the posterior portion of each region was biased to eyes, while the anterior portion was biased to mouth and chin stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Within the occipital and fusiform face processing regions, there exist systematic spatial tuning to different face parts that support further computation combining them.
source: Our results demonstrate that within the occipital and fusiform face processing regions, there exist systematic spatial tuning to different face parts that support further computation combining them.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and represents an inference about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The ventral temporal cortex (VTC) in the brain supports our remarkable ability to recognize objects rapidly and accurately from the visual input in everyday life.
source: The ventral temporal cortex (VTC) in the brain supports our remarkable ability to recognize objects rapidly and accurately from the visual input in everyday life.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of VTC.

claim: Identity information is extracted from visual input through multiple stages of representation.
source: Identity information is extracted from visual input through multiple stages of representation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about visual processing.

claim: Multiple levels of feature representation manifest at different scales of anatomical organizations which are superimposed in the VTC.
source: Numerous studies have already revealed multiple levels of feature representation manifest at different scales of anatomical organizations which superimposed in the VTC.
evidence: This is supported by previous research in the field.

claim: Superordinate category representations (e.g. animate/inanimate, real-world size) manifest at large scale organization covering the whole VTC.
source: The superordinate category representations (e.g. animate/inanimate, real-world size) manifest at large scale organization covering the whole VTC.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about VTC organization.

claim: Category-selective representations (e.g. face, body, and scene selective regions in the mid-fusiform gyrus) are revealed at finer spatial scale in the VTC.
source: Meanwhile, the category-selective representations (e.g. face, body, and scene selective regions in the mid-fusiform gyrus) are revealed at finer spatial scale in the VTC (Hasson et al., 2003; Spiridon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited research studies.

claim: There is a general spatial organization of neural responses to dimensions in object feature space in monkey inferotemporal cortex.
source: Recent evidence suggested a general spatial organization of neural responses to dimensions in object feature space in monkey inferotemporal cortex (Bao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited research study.

claim: Fine-scale spatial organizations of low-level visual features have been found in early visual cortex, such as ocular dominance columns and orientation pinwheels.
source: Fine-scale spatial organizations of low-level visual features have already been found in early visual cortex, such as ocular dominance columns and orientation pinwheels (Blasdel and Salama, 1986; Bonhoeffer and Grinvald, 1991; Hubel et al., 1977; Weliky et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited research studies.

claim: Face-selective neurons in face-selective regions showed different sensitivities to various face features or combinations of dimensions in face feature space.
source: Neurophysiology studies in non-human primates demonstrated face-selective neurons in face-selective regions showed different sensitivities to various of face feature or combination of dimensions in face feature space (Chang and Tsao, 2017; Freiwald et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited neurophysiology studies in non-human primates.

claim: The neural response patterns in FFA or OFA could distinguish different face parts.
source: Human fMRI studies also found the neural response patterns in FFA or OFA could distinguish different face parts (Zhang et al., 2015), suggesting voxels within same face-selective region may have different face feature tuning.
evidence: This is supported by a cited human fMRI study.

claim: Voxels within the same face-selective region may have different face feature tuning.
source: Human fMRI studies also found the neural response patterns in FFA or OFA could distinguish different face parts (Zhang et al., 2015), suggesting voxels within same face-selective region may have different face feature tuning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited research findings.

claim: The spatial distribution of a face feature may be relevant to the physical location of that feature in a face.
source: In addition, previous study also suggests that the spatial distribution of a face feature may be relevant to the physical location of that feature in a face (Henriksson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited previous study.

claim: The sizes of the face-selective regions in VTC are relatively small, spanning about 1 cm.
source: The sizes of the face-selective regions in VTC are relatively small, spanning about 1 cm.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the anatomical size of face-selective regions, based on established knowledge.

claim: High-resolution fMRI with sufficient sensitivity and spatial precision is necessary to investigate the potential spatial tuning within each face region.
source: To investigate the potential spatial tuning within each face region, high-resolution fMRI with sufficient sensitivity and spatial precision is necessary.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the small size of face-selective regions.

claim: Fine-scale patterns have been observed in early visual cortex with high-field fMRI, such as columnar-like structures in V1, V2, V3, V3a, and hMT.
source: With high-field fMRI, fine-scale patterns have been observed in early visual cortex, such as columnar-like structures in V1, V2, V3, V3a, and hMT (Cheng et al., 2001; Goncalves et al., 2015; Nasr et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 2019; Yacoub et al., 2008; Zimmermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited research studies.

claim: High-field fMRI findings validate the feasibility of using high-field fMRI to reveal fine-scale (several mm) structures in the visual cortex.
source: These findings validate the feasibility of using high-field fMRI to reveal fine-scale (several mm) structures in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited findings about high-field fMRI capabilities.

claim: The mid-fusiform sulcus (MFS) is relatively small structure in the VTC, but consistently present in most individuals.
source: MFS is relatively small structure in the VTC, but consistently present in most individuals (Weiner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited research study.

claim: The structure of MFS could predict the coordinates of face-selective region around mid-fusiform, especially the anterior one.
source: On the one hand, the structure of MFS could predict the coordinates of face-selective region around mid-fusiform, especially the anterior one (Weiner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited research study.

claim: MFS is highly consistent with many anatomical lateral-medial transitions in the VTC, such as cytoarchitecture and white-matter connectivity transitions.
source: On the other hand, MFS is found to be highly consistent with many anatomical lateral-medial transitions in the VTC, such as cytoarchitecture and white-matter connectivity transitions (Weiner et al., 2014; Caspers et al., 2013; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014; Lorenz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited research studies.

claim: MFS could predict the transitions in many function organization, such as animacy/inanimacy and face/scene preference.
source: In addition, it could also predict the transitions in many function organization, such as animacy/inanimacy and face/scene preference (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited research study.

claim: Eyes generated higher responses than nose, hair, and chin in all face selective regions except for eyes vs. nose in the left FFA and for eyes vs. chin in left OFA.
source: All face selective regions showed a similar trend that eyes generated higher responses than nose, hair, and chin (ts > 2.61, ps <0.05; except for eyes vs. nose in the left FFA and for eyes vs. chin in left OFA, ts < 2.40, ps >0.06. See Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mouth generated similar response amplitudes as eyes in all face-selective regions.
source: However, mouth generated similar response amplitudes as eyes (ts < 1.58, ps >0.17).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Eyes and mouth are two dominant features in face perception.
source: Considering that eyes and mouth are two dominant features in face perception (Schyns et al., 2002; Wegrzyn et al., 2017), and their response amplitudes were similar in face-selective regions, in the initial step, we compared the spatial patterns of neural responses to eyes with that to mouth within each ROI.
evidence: This is supported by cited research studies.

claim: A spatial pattern was observed in the right pFFA consistently across all participants where the posterior portion was biased to respond more to eyes and the anterior portion was biased to respond more to mouth.
source: A spatial pattern was observed in the right pFFA consistently across all participants (Figure 2). In the dimension parallel to the mid-fusiform gyrus, the posterior portion of the right pFFA was biased to respond more to eyes, whereas the anterior portion was biased to respond more to mouth.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The anatomical orientation of MFS is highly correlated with the spatial tuning of face parts.
source: Note that in participant S2, the direction of MFS was more lateral-medial near the position of the right pFFA, and interestingly, the eyes-mouth contrast map was oriented in the same direction, even though S2's map may initially appear oriented differently from that of other participants. It suggests the anatomical orientation of MFS is highly correlated with such spatial tuning of face parts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation in participant S2's data.

claim: The eyes-mouth biases in the right pFFA show strong reliability within participants.
source: Then we calculated the correlation coefficient between such biases across different voxels between the two data sets to estimate the reliability of the results in the right pFFA. The results demonstrate strong reliability of the data within participants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by split-half reliability analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between the eyes-mouth neural response differences and the position index along the posterior-anterior dimension in the right pFFA.
source: To quantify this trend, we further calculated the correlation coefficient between the eyes-mouth neural response differences and the position index along the posterior-anterior dimension (i.e. more posterior location was assigned with smaller value) in each participant. The group result revealed a significant negative correlation (t(5)=8.36, p = 0.0004, Cohen's d = 3.41), confirming the consistency across participants that the posterior part of right pFFA was biased to eyes and anterior part was biased to mouth.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Non-face objects generated significantly lower but spatially similar patterns of activation compared with faces across the right pFFA.
source: Indeed, non-face objects generated significantly lower but spatially similar patterns of activation compared with faces across the right pFFA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 3C.

claim: There is a general intrinsic BOLD sensitivity profile in the pFFA regardless of the stimuli.
source: This result suggests that there is a general intrinsic BOLD sensitivity profile in the pFFA regardless of the stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that faces and objects generate spatially similar patterns.

claim: Both face and non-face object patterns explained large part of the variation of the face part patterns (for faces average R2 = 0.86, for objects average R2 = 0.72).
source: Indeed, both face and non-face object patterns explained large part of the variation of the face part patterns (for faces average R2 = 0.86, for objects average R2 = 0.72).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of the data.

claim: Results with object patterns removed showed clear posterior bias for eyes and anterior bias for mouth in the right pFFA.
source: Consistently, results with object patterns removed showed clear posterior bias for eyes and anterior bias for mouth in the right pFFA (Figure 3D bottom panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D bottom panel.

claim: All stimuli were presented at the fixation with a 1.3° horizontal jitter either to the left or to the right alternatively in different trials within a block.
source: To control for the potential contribution from retinotopic bias of the different face part conditions, in our experiment, all stimuli were presented at the fixation with a 1.3° horizontal jitter either to the left or to the right alternatively in different trials within a block.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: There were small degrees (less than 3°) of retinotopic differences between the eyes and mouth conditions.
source: Even though the stimuli were centered on the fixation, because of the nature of the face parts (e.g. two eyes are apart, chin depicts the outline of the face), there were still small degrees (less than 3°) of retinotopic differences between the eyes and mouth conditions.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential confound in the experimental design.

claim: In Control Experiment 1, the eye vs. mouth contrast revealed spatial patterns in the right pFFA very similar to that in the main experiment in all participants.
source: In all participants, the eye vs. mouth contrast revealed spatial patterns in the right pFFA very similar to that in the main experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Contrasting fMRI responses between the near central and near peripheral location regardless the face parts failed to reveal consistent patterns across participants in Control Experiment 1.
source: However, contrasting fMRI responses between the near central and near peripheral location regardless the face parts failed to reveal consistent patterns across participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The different fMRI response patterns observed in the right pFFA were contributed by face feature differences rather than retinotopic bias.
source: These results further support that the different fMRI response patterns we observed in the right pFFA were contributed by face feature differences rather than retinotopic bias.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of Control Experiment 1.

claim: Consistent anterior-posterior spatial patterns in the right pFFA were observed in eight participants in Control Experiment 2.
source: With a 2 × 2 design (eyes vs. nose & mouth x present above vs. below fixation) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), consistent anterior-posterior spatial patterns in the right pFFA were observed in eight participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), which further corroborated our main finding of spatially organized representation of face parts in the right pFFA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Generally more voxels in the right pFFA were biased to left visual field.
source: Although generally more voxels in the right pFFA were bias to left visual field, which is consistent with previous report (Kay et al., 2015; Nichols et al., 2016), we observed no consistent spatial pattern in either x or y map of the right pFFA across participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by pRF data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and cited research.

claim: No consistent spatial pattern in either x or y map of the right pFFA was observed across participants in the pRF experiment.
source: Although generally more voxels in the right pFFA were bias to left visual field, which is consistent with previous report (Kay et al., 2015; Nichols et al., 2016), we observed no consistent spatial pattern in either x or y map of the right pFFA across participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The right OFA had distinct response patterns for eyes and mouth along the posterior-anterior dimension.
source: Among these regions, the right OFA also had distinct response patterns for eyes and mouth along the posterior-anterior dimension (Figure 4), similar to what we observed in the right pFFA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Group negative correlation was observed between the eyes-mouth differences and the posterior-anterior location of the right OFA.
source: Group negative correlation was observed between the eyes-mouth differences and the posterior-anterior location of the right OFA (t(5)=3.63, p = 0.015, Cohen's d = 1.48).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Similar spatial patterns between eyes-mouth bias and visual field bias in vertical direction were observed in the right OFA.
source: We also observed similar spatial patterns between eyes-mouth bias and visual field bias in vertical direction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with previous findings in inferior occipital gyrus (de Haas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and supported by a cited study.

claim: The right pFFA may receive face feature information from right OFA for further processing.
source: This is consistent with, but adds some constraints to, the idea that the right pFFA may receive face feature information from right OFA for further processing (Liu et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference supported by the current findings and cited research.

claim: In other face-selective regions (right aFFA, left FFA, left OFA), no consistent pattern was observed for eyes-mouth differences along the posterior-anterior dimension.
source: In other face-selective regions, no consistent pattern was observed, as the correlations between the eyes-mouth difference and posterior-anterior location were not significant (ts <1.09, ps >0.32, see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Chin and mouth elicited similar response patterns along the anterior-posterior dimension in the right pFFA and right OFA after regressing out general spatial patterns.
source: Chin and mouth elicited similar response patterns along the anterior-posterior dimension in the right pFFA and right OFA after regressing out general spatial patterns (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: By directly contrasting fMRI response patterns between eyes and chin, similar spatial profiles were revealed in the right pFFA and right OFA that the posterior part was biased to eyes and anterior part was biased to chin.
source: By directly contrasting fMRI response patterns between eyes and chin, similar spatial profiles were revealed in the right pFFA and right OFA that the posterior part was biased to eyes and anterior part was biased to chin (ts >5.30, ps <0.01, see Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A similar though less obvious profile for eyes vs. chin was observed in the left FFA.
source: We also observed a similar though less obvious profile in the left FFA (t(5)=2.68, p = 0.04, Cohen's d = 1.09), but not in the right aFFA or left OFA (ts <0.41, ps >0.71).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Within certain face-selective regions in the human occipito-temporal cortex, the neural representations of different facial features have consistent spatial profiles.
source: Our results reveal that within certain face-selective regions in the human occipito-temporal cortex, the neural representations of different facial features have consistent spatial profiles.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the experimental data.

claim: Fine-scale spatial tuning is found similarly in the right pFFA and right OFA, but not in the more anterior right aFFA nor in the left hemisphere's face-selective regions.
source: Such fine-scale spatial tuning is found similarly in the right pFFA and right OFA, but not in the more anterior right aFFA nor in the left hemisphere's face-selective regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the experimental data.

claim: Fine-scale spatial tuning for face parts exists at the early to intermediate stages of face processing hierarchy in the right hemisphere.
source: In other words, fine-scale spatial tuning for face parts exists at the early to intermediate stages of face processing hierarchy in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings about which regions show spatial tuning.

claim: Eyes and mouth showed most distinct spatial profiles in the right pFFA and right OFA among the five face parts tested.
source: In the current study, five face parts (i.e. eyes, nose, mouth, hair, and chin) were tested, with eyes and mouth showed most distinct spatial profiles in the right pFFA and right OFA.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The nose and hair stimuli elicited lower fMRI responses compared with eyes and mouth stimuli.
source: For one, the nose and hair stimuli elicited lower fMRI responses compared with eyes and mouth stimuli, making it more difficult to detect potential spatial patterns.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data.

claim: Eyes and mouth provide more information about faces than other features in face processing.
source: The observation that eyes and mouth elicited most differential patterns is consistent with them providing more information about faces than other features in face processing (Schyns et al., 2002; Wegrzyn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited research studies.

claim: The dominance of eyes and mouth in face-selective regions could be considered as a form of cortical magnification of more informative features.
source: The dominance of eyes and mouth in face-selective regions could be considered as a form of cortical magnification of more informative features, a common principle of functional organization in sensory cortex (Cowey and Rolls, 1974; Daniel and Whitteridge, 1961; Penfield and Boldrey, 1937).
evidence: This is an inference supported by cited research on cortical magnification principles.

claim: In the inferior occipital gyrus, where the OFA is located, there are both tunings for retinotopic location and face parts.
source: A recent study has revealed that in the inferior occipital gyrus, where the OFA located, both tunings for retinotopic location and face parts (de Haas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a cited recent study.

claim: The two tuning maps (retinotopic and face parts) were correlated within individuals in the inferior occipital gyrus.
source: Although the tuning peak maps were idiosyncratic across individuals, the two tuning maps were correlated within individuals, suggesting a relationship between face parts configuration and their typical retinotopic configuration.
evidence: This is supported by a cited recent study.

claim: There exists a consistent spatial profile of face part tuning across individuals in the OFA.
source: Our findings provide additional support for face part turning in the OFA, and further reveal that there exists a consistent spatial profile of face part tuning across individuals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: Although the organization of feature tuning could be constrained by the retinotopic tuning in occipital cortex, a more abstract feature tuning could still be spatially organized in cortical areas with absent or minimal retinotopic property in the later stages of VTC.
source: More importantly, our finding of spatial tuning of face part in the pFFA indicates that although the organization of feature tuning could be constrained by the retinotopic tuning in occipital cortex, a more abstract feature tuning could still be spatially organized in cortical areas with absent or minimal retinotopic property in the later stages of VTC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings about spatial tuning in pFFA.

claim: In the OFA and FFA, the differences between neural response patterns of face parts were correlated with physical distances between face parts in a face.
source: Their results showed that in the OFA and FFA, the differences between neural response patterns of face parts were correlated with physical distances between face parts in a face.
evidence: This is supported by a cited previous study (Henriksson et al., 2015).

claim: The possible mechanism underlying faciotopy organization is the local-to-global computation, where physically adjacent face parts interact more than parts far apart from each other during the early stages of processing.
source: The possible mechanism underlying such faciotopy organization is the local-to-global computation, that physically adjacent face parts interact more than parts far apart from each other during the early stages of processing, thus it is more efficient for them to have neural representations near each other.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed patterns.

claim: Hair is generally less invariant and less informative in face identification.
source: However, in the current study, we did not find the posterior bias pattern for hair as we did for eyes, even though hair and eyes are spatially adjacent, which could be caused by the hair being generally less invariant and less informative in the face identification.
evidence: This is an inference to explain why hair did not show the expected pattern.

claim: The mouth region provides more information for language processing and audio-visual communication perception.
source: Specifically, the mouth region provides more information for language processing and audio-visual communication perception, thus it may be more connected to the language processing system.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about the functional role of the mouth.

claim: The eyes are more important in face detection and eye gaze signifies interest, thus it may be more connected to the attention system.
source: Meanwhile, the eyes are more important in face detection and eye gaze signifies interest, thus it may be more connected to the attention system.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about the functional role of the eyes.

claim: Connectivity profiles could predict the functional selectivity in the VTC.
source: Previous studies have already found the connectivity profiles could predict the functional selectivity in the VTC, thus it would be interesting to examine whether the face part spatial tuning in the pFFA could be predicted using functional or anatomical connectivity to the other brain regions in the future studies.
evidence: This is based on previous research findings.

claim: The FFA is overlapped with body-selective region fusiform-body area (FBA).
source: As the FFA is overlapped with body-selective region fusiform-body area (FBA), it is possible that some face features (e.g. mouth) could be represented closer to the FBA, while face parts such as the eyes are more represented in the FFA proper.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the organization of VTC.

claim: Existing evidence does not support a consistent anterior-posterior relationship between FFA and FBA.
source: However, existing evidence does not support a consistent anterior-posterior relationship between FFA and FBA (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited research study.

claim: The spatial clustering of neurons with similar tuning is one of the organization principles in the brain.
source: The spatial clustering of neurons with similar tuning is one of the organization principles in the brain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about brain organization.

claim: Spatial clustering may optimize the efficiency of the neural computation by reducing the total wire length.
source: Such clustering may optimize the efficiency of the neural computation by reducing the total wire length (Laughlin and Sejnowski, 2003), thus the clustering of neurons with similar feature tuning within face-selective regions could improve the processing efficiency to face stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by a cited research study.

claim: The clustering of neurons with similar feature tuning within face-selective regions could improve the processing efficiency to face stimuli.
source: Such clustering may optimize the efficiency of the neural computation by reducing the total wire length (Laughlin and Sejnowski, 2003), thus the clustering of neurons with similar feature tuning within face-selective regions could improve the processing efficiency to face stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited principle and the current findings.

claim: There is strong correspondence between fMRI signal and neuronal responses in monkey face processing network.
source: Previous fMRI and single unit recording studies in monkey face processing network have demonstrated strong correspondence between fMRI signal and neuronal responses (Tsao et al., 2006), suggesting that the face part tuning in our results may be driven by neuronal response biases.
evidence: This is supported by a cited research study.

claim: The face part tuning observed in the results may be driven by neuronal response biases.
source: Previous fMRI and single unit recording studies in monkey face processing network have demonstrated strong correspondence between fMRI signal and neuronal responses (Tsao et al., 2006), suggesting that the face part tuning in our results may be driven by neuronal response biases.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research and the current findings.

claim: Face parts are believed to be represented in the posterior regions such as the OFA in the face processing network.
source: In the face processing network, face parts are believed to be represented in the posterior regions such as the OFA (Liu et al., 2010; Arcurio et al., 2012; Pitcher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited research studies.

claim: Part information is transmitted to anterior regions to be further integrated to form holistic face representations.
source: Part information is transmitted to anterior regions to be further integrated to form holistic face representations (Zhang et al., 2015; Rotshtein et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited research studies.

claim: The more anterior regions in the face processing network are more responsible for representing integrated face information such as gender or identity rather than individual face parts.
source: In that sense, the more anterior regions in the face processing network are more responsible for representing integrated face information such as gender or identity rather than individual face parts (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Landi and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited research studies.

claim: At the right aFFA, there is no obvious spatial tuning of face parts.
source: Consistent with this idea, at the right aFFA, there is no obvious spatial tuning of face parts.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings.

claim: A clear hemispheric difference was found that the distinct spatial response patterns for face parts were observed in the right but not the left hemisphere.
source: Meanwhile, a clear hemispheric difference was found in our results that the distinct spatial response patterns for face parts were observed in the right but not the left hemisphere, which is consistent with previous findings that compared with left FFA, right FFA is more sensitive to face specific features (Meng et al., 2012) and configural information (Rossion et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings and supported by cited research.

claim: Compared with left FFA, right FFA is more sensitive to face specific features.
source: Meanwhile, a clear hemispheric difference was found in our results that the distinct spatial response patterns for face parts were observed in the right but not the left hemisphere, which is consistent with previous findings that compared with left FFA, right FFA is more sensitive to face specific features (Meng et al., 2012) and configural information (Rossion et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited research studies.

claim: Right FFA is more sensitive to configural information compared with left FFA.
source: Meanwhile, a clear hemispheric difference was found in our results that the distinct spatial response patterns for face parts were observed in the right but not the left hemisphere, which is consistent with previous findings that compared with left FFA, right FFA is more sensitive to face specific features (Meng et al., 2012) and configural information (Rossion et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited research studies.

claim: One of the neural mechanisms underlying the functional lateralization of face processing could be the existence of spatial clustering of face part tunings in the right hemisphere.
source: Therefore, one of the neural mechanisms underlying the functional lateralization of face processing could be the existence of spatial clustering of face part tunings in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings.

claim: A large number of features are represented for object recognition.
source: Consequently, we now believe that a large number of features are represented for object recognition, but how does our brain physically organize such complex feature representations in the VTC?
evidence: This is based on current understanding in the field.

claim: Feature representations manifest in different spatial scales, with more general features at large spatial scale across the whole VTC and more specific features at finer spatial scales within specific object processing regions.
source: One possible solution is that these feature representations manifest in different spatial scales. For more general features the representation manifests at large spatial scale across the whole VTC (e.g. large/small, animate/inanimate), and for more specific features such as face parts, it manifests at finer spatial scales within specific object processing regions.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework proposed based on the findings.

claim: 20 unique front-view Asian male face images were used for face stimuli in the main experiment.
source: In the main experiment, for face stimuli, 20 unique front-view Asian male face images were used.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each face image was divided into five parts (eyes, nose, mouth, hair, and chin).
source: Each face image was gray-scaled and further divided into five parts (i.e. eyes, nose, mouth, hair, and chin. See Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The full face and object images on average subtended around 5° x 7°.
source: The full face and object images on average subtended around 5° x 7°.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli properties.

claim: Each main experimental run contained two blocks of each stimulus condition.
source: Each main experimental run contained two blocks of each stimulus condition.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each stimulus block lasted 16 s and contained 20 images of the same type.
source: Each stimulus block lasted 16 s and contained 20 images of the same type.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each image was presented for 600 ms followed by a 200 msec blank interval.
source: Each image was presented for 600 ms at fixation and followed by a 200 msec blank interval.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: There was a 16 s blank fixation block at the beginning, the middle, and the end of each run.
source: There was a 16 s blank fixation block at the beginning, the middle, and the end of each run.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants performed a 1-back task during the scan.
source: Participants performed a 1-back task that they were asked to press a button when two successive images were the same.
evidence: This describes the experimental task.

claim: Six participants (3 females) were recruited in the main experiment.
source: Six (3 females) human participants were recruited in the main experiment.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: All participants were between the ages of 21 and 27, right-handed, and had normal or corrected to normal visual acuity.
source: All participants were between the ages of 21 and 27, right-handed, and had normal or corrected to normal visual acuity.
evidence: This describes the participant characteristics.

claim: MRI data were collected on Siemens Magnetom 7 Tesla MRI system.
source: MRI data were collected on Siemens Magnetom 7 Tesla MRI system (passively shielded, 45mT/s slew rate) (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany), with a 32-channel receive 1-channel transmit head coil (NOVA Medical, Inc, Wilmington, MA, USA), at the Beijing MRI Center for Brain Research (BMCBR).
evidence: This describes the scanning equipment.

claim: High-resolution T1-weighted anatomical images were acquired with 0.7 mm isotropic voxel size.
source: High-resolution T1-weighted anatomical images (0.7 mm isotropic voxel size) were acquired with a MPRAGE sequence (256 sagittal slices, acquisition matrix = 320 × 320, Field of view = 223 × 223 mm, GRAPPA factor = 3, TR = 3100ms, TE = 3.56ms, TI = 1250ms, flip angle = 5°, pixel bandwidth = 182 Hz per pixel).
evidence: This describes the scanning parameters.

claim: GE-EPI sequences were used to collect functional data with 1.2 mm isotropic voxels.
source: GE-EPI sequences was used to collect functional data in the main experiment (TR = 2000ms, TE = 18ms, 1.2 mm isotropic voxels, FOV = 168 × 168 mm, image matrix = 140 × 140, GRAPPA factor = 3, partial Fourier 6/8, 31 slices of 1.2 mm thinkness, flip angle is about 80, pixel bandwidth = 1276 Hz per pixel).
evidence: This describes the scanning parameters.

claim: Dielectric pads were placed on both sides of the head to improve B1 efficiency in the temporal cortex.
source: Dielectric pads were placed on both sides of the head to improve B1 efficiency in the temporal cortex (Teeuwisse et al., 2012), while bite-bar was used to reduce head movements for each participant.
evidence: This describes the scanning procedure, with citation supporting the use of dielectric pads.

claim: Bite-bar was used to reduce head movements for each participant.
source: Dielectric pads were placed on both sides of the head to improve B1 efficiency in the temporal cortex (Teeuwisse et al., 2012), while bite-bar was used to reduce head movements for each participant.
evidence: This describes the scanning procedure.

claim: FFA and OFA were defined as the set of continuous voxels in fusiform gyrus and inferior occipital gyrus, respectively, that showed significantly higher response to faces than to objects (p < 0.01, uncorrected).
source: Specifically, FFA and OFA was defined as the set of continuous voxels in fusiform gyrus and inferior occipital gyrus, respectively, that showed significantly higher response to faces than to objects (p < 0.01, uncorrected).
evidence: This describes the ROI definition procedure.

claim: Right pFFA, right anterior FFA (right aFFA), right OFA, and left FFA were identified in all six participants.
source: We were able to identify right pFFA, right anterior FFA (right aFFA), right OFA, and left FFA in all six participants.
evidence: This describes the ROI identification results.

claim: The left OFA was successfully identified in five out of six participants.
source: The left OFA were successfully identified in five out of six participants.
evidence: This describes the ROI identification results.

claim: Voxels with signal changes to face stimuli larger than 4% were excluded to remove the vein signal in the functional data.
source: In each ROI, to remove the vein signal in the functional data, voxels of which signal changes to face stimuli were larger than 4% were excluded in further analysis.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing procedure.
